I'm trying to figure out why it wouldn't be fair to base rankings on victory
points? You're still trying to run up as many victory points as you can in
every game. It's still the second level tiebreaker to determine who makes
the finals - and with game wins being very small integers, VPs will often come
into play. And in the finals the game win rule means nothing at all. Only
victory points are important - yet the finals count as much as any other
games do for purposes of rankings.

Generally, I guess you'd like to see that the people who make the finals most
often are the same as the highest ranked people but it's not strictly necessary.
It isn't always true right now for at least a couple of reasons: due to the
ratings from the final games themselves and due to people who often score just
under what they need to make the finals vs. people who either flop horribly or
do terrifically and make the finals. And I'm pretty sure that in the future,
it will continue to be true in the vast majority of cases anyway, in spite or
your concerns about your ranking relative to Mr. Peal.

I would make it tantamount to (though not as egregious as) collusion and
punish it in a similar manner. Because, in effect, that's what it is. The
fact that it happens in game is irrelevant, though it does make it so that it's
not as steep an offense. Sitting there and saying "Well, if you let me oust
these two people (or this person and withdraw or whatever) and I'll help
you get those VPs then I'll roll over and die to give you my VP" is a form
of collusion.

With "game wins" being the determining factor, you can have a situation
where 1 person has 4 VPs and 2 game wins and another has 5 VPs 1
game win. The guy with 5 VPs doesn't get into the final while the 4 VP
guy squeeks in. How is that fair? I don't care how remote a possiblity
that is, the simple fact that it can (and probably will) occur is enough to
not have it as an option.

One of the new rules that go hand in hand with the "game wins" rule
that I don't like is the one where you *must* maximize your VPs and
not do anything outside those boundries (paraphrase). That basically
ties your hands and makes it so that you can't do alot of things that
might ensure your survival. For example, it is frowned upon (if not
outright disallowed, though I could be wrong about that) working to
oust your predator to make sure that you can stay alive. Granted,
you don't get the VP for your predator's oust, but you do make it so
that you could survive and go on to get VPs of your own. If you are
out of the game, there is absolutely NO chance that you'll ever get a
VP. However, while you are still in it, there's always a chance. It's
the same argument I had with Ben Peal one year at Dragon*Con.

Messages.Author: Steve Wampler
Messages.Body:
I haven't been on this group here in years, but, well, I have an opinion and a net
connection at the same time again, so here goes....

Sorrow wrote:

> > >Making deals it help increase your (chances of getting) VPs is one thing.

> if it is where one is the predator of the other, then it's always going to be that
> one concedes his or her position as part of the deal. There's no way around it.
> This is a form of collusion and should be made illegal.

I know there was an argument about the definition of collusion recently, but its one
of those things that tournament players can't just agree to disagree about; everyone
agrees that "collusion", whatever it is, is cheating and needs to be disallowed. You
are certainly entitled to your opinion that a deal which involves allowing yourself
to be ousted is automatically collusion. I just think you are wrong.
Dealmaking is entirely within the spirit of the VTES world and perfectly allowable
under the rules. Pretty much everyone agrees that deals along the lines of "vote for
my krc and I'll vote for your con boon" are legal. A player is allowed to do what is
necessary to increase his or her own chances of winning. Sometimes this requires
trading favors with another player. Dealmaking is a skill, one which VTES rewards.
The problem is that they introduce the possibilty of the game being affected by
things other than player skill, like "vote for my krc and I'll trade you that rare
card you want" or "vote for my con boon because we're both from Chicago and you'd
rather that I win than some guy you don't know". Such arrangements are "collusion"
and should clearly be banned from competetive play. Fortunately, the fact that they
include elements from outside the game makes them easy to identify, and thus easy to
ban.
Personally, I see table splitting arrangements as deals of the first type. They
include only in game elements. They exist to maximize the VPs gained by each person
in the deal. A player who can get three VPs without help is not going to make a deal
with another player in which he or she gains only two. Sure, it sucks for the other
players at the table, but they don't have to sit there and take it - there are three
of them after all. If they can't between them take on two other players, then they
weren't going to win anyway.
The main complaint I have heard about such table splitting propositions is that they
invaraibly involve one player "rolling over" and being ousted intentionally, to give
VPs to the other partner in the deal. People have called this "unsportsmanlike", on
the grounds that all players should fight on to the bitter end in order to gain the
most points possible. However, I consider this argument to be shortsighted. Sure, a
player might stand to gain more VPs by breaking th deal at the end and not allowing
himself to be ousted. However, if the table is such at the start of the game that
that player has NO chance of getting ANY vps, then getting 2 vps from such a deal is
indeed "sportsmanlike" - it is playing to win, within the confines of the rules.

> I do not see how this
> would be overly difficult to disallow.
> Again, I think the "game wins" system was a poor choice for an alternative.
>

Again, your viewpoint baffles me. What could possibly be more fair in a tournament
than rewarding wins? This is how pretty much every tournament for every other game
under the sun works. In Magic, victory is determined my opponents defeated, not
total damage inflicted. Chess tournaments are won by he who wins the most games, not
he who removes the most total pieces. The game wins system will mean a change in the
way tournaments work, but the change makes the system more intuitive.

-Steve Wampler

Sometimes it is, sometimes it isn't. In my experience, more than 3/4 of the
time, it *actually* is collusion - not just "in effect" is collusion.
Correctly, it should be be sanctioned by the tournament judge when it happens.
But no one ever calls the judge over, though, because it would involve the
judge ruling that one player or (in the case of a 2-2 or 2-2-1 tie) both
players are settling for less than a win when he (or they) have a realistic
chance to win. That ruling is subjective and incredibly arguable. Most
players simply want to play the game, not sit around debating a subjective
question which has no provable answer.

So here's the problem with your suggestion: it's already been done. And it
doesn't work. Even if it were written into the rules that players could not
agree on a table split, I suspect there would be gray areas and those gray
areas would become holes through players could drive Volkswagens through.
The thing I like about the "Game Wins" rule is that there's no getting
around it with fancy talking. Split it anyway you like, only one player
can have the game win and that's the important thing.

This analysis is true for /all/ deals. Consider something which is pretty
clearly an allowable deal: "Player A will bum's rush a vampire belonging to

deal is also base on trust. It is not in player B's interest to use a minion

have a large effect on the game.

potence IG rush decks. If they fought each other, they would both die. The

forward, and gain some VPs. But his predator needs to get something out of the
deal, or it isn't any good for him. So they agree to share the VPs available at
the table. The prey goes forward, gain 3, then rolls over. This is not the same
as suicide, because we saw that in the "normal" case, this player would be dead

damage in some form or other. Many decks cannot do much cross-table
damage -- straightforward bleed decks, bruise/bleed decks, etc. These

being in the "carved up" portion of the table.

sitting as predator/prey. A POT deck who doesn't have to worry about
his predator can completely erase his prey. A POT deck who doesn't need

two decks aimed at him -- he will only have got a VP if he's a
super-fast bleed deck, and otherwise the table will just be filled with
vamps in torpor. Then, the "prey" POT deck bleeds people out one by
one, while the "predator" deck kills any vampires that leave torpor or
are influenced out.

(with vote decks) -- the ability to demolish the table is only magnified
when you're able to direct your ally's actions to your own benefit.

it's quite probable that their decks will not be able to significantly
affect you. And they shouldn't be forced to band together in the first
place -- they should be allowed to just play their decks if they so
choose.

good chance of getting the rest. Player D can't offer players B and C
anything in return, really, because of the following "gotcha": if
player D makes a deal with B to give C's and his own VP to B, then
player C will no longer go along with the OTHER part of the deal, as he
gets screwed either way. Same if player D makes a deal with C.

screwed and will not cooperate.

Alliance(tm) end up going "out for themselves" to try to snag as much as
they can out from under The Alliance's nose. And the Alliance ends up
facing a 2 on 1 on 1 on 1 instead of a 2 on 3, and wins.

needed to be beaten down.

The game and the real world do not have the same ethical code. If I
punch you on the nose in the real world, then this will usually be
both illegal and contrary to Christian ethics (YMMV). If I do the
same thing in a boxing match then this is not just permitted, it is
expected. In the real world, if you make a deal with someone, then
it is expected to be binding, both in law and as a matter of personal
honour. But, in the game, deals are not binding and so you should
break them if they get in the way of the game's objective. If you
refuse do so so for the sake of real-world ethics ("my word is my
bond") then this is muddled thinking - failure to understand that you
are no longer supposed to be in the real world but are in the World of
Darkness instead. If you refuse to break deals for the sake of your
metagame reputation ("if I break this deal then he won't deal with me

out-of-game relationship ahead of your in-game one.

playing the game.

what do you actually plan to do now if you find yourself playing Rush
with Rush as your prey? And what do you do in ordinary, one-off games
where tournament rules and scoring do not apply?

Mr Taubman thought that he'd covered his tracks well by writing
nothing down. He didn't reckon on his CEO ratting on him. Maybe he
shouldn't have said that she'd "look good in stripes". <grin> The
authorities in this case decided that it was feasible to make the case
stick. It's mostly a matter of political will. If you make an
example of a high profile offender, then it encourages others to
follow the rules. If you fail do so then you get something like the
Magic tournament scene which, by many accounts, used to be quite
corrupt with many cases of rampant cheating being winked at.

sanctioned or regulated by the game rules - it's just some table talk.
There's never a valid in-game reason for committing suicide - it's
contrary to the specified objective and to the general spirit of the
game - a Machiavellian power struggle.

>allies of its own, then /you/ need to "suck it up and take it like a man."

emphasis on sweeping tables and more on just getting your nose in
front to take the win. This may make for a metagame in which the
three targets of the rush decks are indeed better able to look after
themselves in combat.

rush decks to proliferate. What happens when you have more than two
of them in a tournament game? From reports here, it sounds like the
game gets ugly. I still think that the ultimate answer is to ban Bum
Rush. <grin>

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Brian wrote:
>>Table splitting was also determined to be unfair to those not included
in the deal, and will soon be illegal.>>

I don't believe it will be illegal, just not a good idea. If getting 2 VPs in
the 2-3 split doesn't get you a table win, there is limited incentive to
attempt it.

>>It was understood that the rules allowed for it. The question was
whether they should have.>>

There is no way to prevent it outright (as it isn't collusion), so making a
"table win" rule that discurages a 3-2 table split is certainly a way to
discourage it, but I'm sure it will still occasionally happen.

>>At what cost? If the other three players are denied a reasonable
chance of victory, and this happens every round, and they give up
tournament V:TES, was it worth it? What if I bring 8 players to your
tourney, and we all play the same type of rush deck, just to do this
every game?>>

That falls under the rubric of collusion, which is specifically illegal.

>>Each player must be presented with some hope for victory, or the game
loses its appeal. With the above example, only the people on "Team
Brian" have a reasonable hope for victory.>>

Depends on the seating. Everyone seems to think that this 3-2 table split thing
is some sort of epidemic. It really isn't--it just shouldn't come up that much.
To pull it off, you need to have two players who are certain that they can't
get any VPs unless they try and split. This doesn't come up that much. If I
feel I can kill my prey, I'll kill him. If my prey feels I can't hurt him, he
won't make a deal (as if I can't hurt him, he is likely to get more than 3
VPs).

>>I disagree. I say it is unethical to live up to any agreement which
is in itself unethical.>>

You are free to say anything you like--I am yet to be convinced that making a
3-2 table split deal, under the current (until January) tournament rules is
unethical. The rules encourage maximizing VPs. Some times the only way to
maximize your VPs is to split 3-2.

>>You have offered the table-split option as preferable to each of 5
alternatives, which suggests to me that it is indeed too powerful,
crippling other strategies and homogenizing gameplay.>>

Nope. It doesn't come up all that often. If I can hurt you, I'm not going to
sacrifice my position to give you more VPs. If I can't hurt you, you have no
incentive to take a deal, and I have no leverage for making such a deal. The
factors neccessary to make such a deal both lucrative and viable are few and
far between.

Andrew wrote:
>>If you commit suicide to help a weaker player then you are not
maximising your victory points.>>

You are in the sense that without the deal, you were getting zero VPs. Rolling
over after getting three VPs gets you three VPs. Thus, maximizing VPs.

>> That's precisely why it is currently illegal.>>

Maximizing VPs isn't manditaory, it is just what he rules encourage. If it were
*illegal* to not maximize VPs, it would be illegal to play a bad deck, which it
is not.

>>Both are against the rules. But there's little need to punish a
player who is resigning - declining to play out a hopeless position.
One should save serious sanction for the players that deserve it - the
table-splitters.>>

How are they against the rules? It is not illegal to oust yourself. It is not
illegal to play and not get any VPs. The rules exist to encourage maximizing
your VPs, but they do not make it illegal to not do this--again, otherwise, it
would be illegal to play a bad deck--certainly there is a deck you could be
playing that could get more VPs, isn't there?

>>Thay are deliberately trying to cheat the system.>>

How? They are trying to maximize their VPs, which the rules exist to encourage.

>>The game and the real world do not have the same ethical code. If I
punch you on the nose in the real world, then this will usually be
both illegal and contrary to Christian ethics (YMMV). If I do the
same thing in a boxing match then this is not just permitted, it is
expected. In the real world, if you make a deal with someone, then
it is expected to be binding, both in law and as a matter of personal
honour. But, in the game, deals are not binding and so you should
break them if they get in the way of the game's objective.>>

This deal doesn't get in the way with the objective of the game. It gets you
more VPs that you would have gotten without the deal.

>>Not necessarily - a boxer might take a dive to avoid getting hurt.
This is understandable but you shouldn't go in the ring if that's how
you feel. You're expected to make a fight of it before you throw in
the towel. Failure to fight when you are able to do so is just not
playing the game.>>

That is not taking a dive at the request of your opponent. Different issue all

>>I'm not convinced - 2 VPs is better than nothing, as you say. But
what do you actually plan to do now if you find yourself playing Rush
with Rush as your prey?>>

Might make a deal, might not. Depends on what else is at the table.

>>And what do you do in ordinary, one-off games where tournament rules and
scoring do not apply?>>

I don't make such deals, as there is zero incentive to do so in non tournament
play.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Andrew wrote:
>>The tournament rules say that you're supposed to play towards the
objective of the game and that is to score more VP than any other
player. Helping someone else win is clearly contrary to that
objective. The quid pro quo (ousting yourself) is a lesser offense
because it typically occurs after the game is decided. You should
really stop play once one player has 3 out of 5 VP. That would make
the self-oust issue moot.>>

It isn't clearly contrary--the rules say get as many VPs as you can, and get
more than anyone else. If you get 3 VPs, you have succedded in that goal. Sure,
you could go on and try for 4 VPs, if not 5, but the only reason you got 3 is
'cause of the deal you made in the first place. If living up to a deal still
gets you 3 VPs and more than anyone else, you have done all you are required to
do.

>>I don't think it's possible to construct a deck which incapable of
scoring VPs and winning the game, is it? There is no way to say with
certainty whether one deck is better than another and so the point is
moot.>>

Of course there is a way to say with certainty that one deck is objectively
better than another. I have a Malk S+B deck with 35 various Dom bleed cards, 25
various Steath Cards, 20 various Master cards, and a crypt vampires averaging
around 5 capacity, all with Dom and Obf. You have a Malk S+B deck that has 5
Threats, 80 Night Moves, 5 Gird Minions, and a crypt that consists of 12
Roxxane, Retrix of the 13th Floors. Deck A is simply better than deck B.

I see people all the time in tournaments playing bad decks--decks that I would
never in a million years consider worth playing, 'cause they aren't any good.
Maybe it is because they are new to the game and don't know any better. Maybe
they just like playing experimental decks. Whatever. Regardless, that they are
playing a bad deck is deleterious to the game--whomever their prey is will get
a free ride and have a noticable advantage. Sure, it is understandable in many
cases (i.e. with a new player) and not something that you can legislate
against, but it certainly is something that affects a given game in a negative
sense. Hmm. Much like how many view a certain other point of discussion on the
table...

>>The game rules include a procedure for withdrawing from the game. And
the tournament rules provide a procedure for conceding. "Giving up"
in some other way is therefore illegal.>>

No it isn't. That is completely absurd. There is nothing in the rules that
prohibit influencing out more vampires than you can afford ("But I *need* this
extra vampire even though it brings me down to 1 pool!"). There is nothing in
the rules that prevent you from not taking any actions ("I need to block!").
People do this all the time without specifically planning to give up--it is
just bad play. There are no rules governing bad play (just like there aren't
any rules governing bad deck design) and the line between bad play and simply
giving up are too thin to look for.

>>It's good that there is some common ground between us.>>

See, again here I have reason to believe you have some sort of deranged view of
me, that is simply not accurate. I don't go to tournaments and make 3-2 table
splits in every game, and laugh at all the people I screw over. I believe in my
years of competetive VTES, I have made a table split one time, ever (as the guy
who got the 2 VPs...) And boy, was Aaron pissed :-) A couple of games I have
played involved weird deals with people that involved them ousting themselves,
but other than that first example, they all involved a sort of "hey--let me get
one VP, guy who has 3 already, and then I'll kill myself, 'cause it gets you 4
anyways and it'll be easier than trying to oust me" deal. Not table splits.
They don't come up all that often, they are difficult to arrange, and usually
simply not a good idea, let alone viable.

I fully understand that table splitting pisses people off and is contrary to
the intent of the game (yet still occasionally a good idea to attempt), but
previous to the Jan 1 tournament rules, there was no strictly definable way
that they were illegal, and even after the "table-wins" rule becomes in effect,
they simply become much less attractive rather than illegal.

On 23 Dec 2001 14:20:38 GMT, Peter D Bakija wrote:

>It isn't clearly contrary--the rules say get as many VPs as you can, and get
>more than anyone else. If you get 3 VPs, you have succedded in that goal. Sure,
>you could go on and try for 4 VPs, if not 5, but the only reason you got 3 is
>'cause of the deal you made in the first place. If living up to a deal still
>gets you 3 VPs and more than anyone else, you have done all you are required to
>do.

The rules say that the players score victory points for doing various
things. They say that the player with the most victory points is the
"winner". They explain how you can play for ante and so win or lose
cards. The last part is quite clear but nobody plays that way.
Otherwise, one might suppose that winning is the only thing that
matters but folk like you and LSJ keep saying that the object is to
maximise VPs even though, so far as I can see, the rules say no such
thing.

These three objectives are multi-dimensional. For example, suppose
that you have 1 VP and no-one else has any. You are currently winning
the game. If winning the game is what matters then you want to keep
things that way. But if maximising VPs is the object of the game then
you might want to score another VP even if this means that another
player does even better and you end up losing 2-3. Play with ante too
and you obviously get a weighting of VPs, depending on the ante cards
associated with them.

Alan Kwan posed the issue of the game's objective over 5 years ago but
didn't get much response. In practise, the matter is still
unresolved. If real players are prepared to do losing deals in the
final of a tournament then, AFAIC, this is broken.

>Of course there is a way to say with certainty that one deck is objectively
>better than another. I have a Malk S+B deck with 35 various Dom bleed cards, 25
>various Steath Cards, 20 various Master cards, and a crypt vampires averaging
>around 5 capacity, all with Dom and Obf. You have a Malk S+B deck that has 5
>Threats, 80 Night Moves, 5 Gird Minions, and a crypt that consists of 12
>Roxxane, Retrix of the 13th Floors. Deck A is simply better than deck B.

You can say this in a 2-player game but VTES is normally multi-player.
Once you have players deliberately joining forces against decks that
appear to be strong then strength can become weakness and vice versa.
You also have the scissors/paper/stone issue. You therefore cannot
construct a strength function for a deck which independent of the
circumstances in which it finds itself.

>No it isn't. That is completely absurd. There is nothing in the rules that
>prohibit influencing out more vampires than you can afford ("But I *need* this
>extra vampire even though it brings me down to 1 pool!").

This is the defense of the rules-lawyer. In the situation where one
player is stronger than the other, a deliberate suicide by the strong
player is clear enough. As a judge, I would have little hesitation in
ruling against this and penalising one or both players for collusion.

>I fully understand that table splitting pisses people off and is contrary to
>the intent of the game (yet still occasionally a good idea to attempt), but
>previous to the Jan 1 tournament rules, there was no strictly definable way
>that they were illegal, and even after the "table-wins" rule becomes in effect,
>they simply become much less attractive rather than illegal.

It seems that you're just fighting some nit-picking point about strict
definitions. This is not really the point - we're talking about
what's right or wrong and you seem to understand that well enough. Mr
Taubman is not just on his way to prison because of the form of words
in a statute. His conviction also depended upon the opinion of the
judge and jury. It's not possible to regulate such matters in a
completely algorithmic manner and that's why VTES has judges too.

Andrew

This is a factor of any multiplayer game where there is a quantifiable way of
determining a finishing place.

In general terms, comparisons of the play of each deck over a period of
time. This will, of course, still be limited but it will be as close to
objective as can be easily ascertained.

A secondary method - equally useful in its own fashion - is pouring over
the deck-list, with a fine tooth-comb, taking into account different
facets, seeing where the deck can be exploited. A deck which, when
examined in that manner, has a relatively secure method of advance and
relatively few exploits may well be a better way of determining this.

(This sort of thing has been going on for years. The old articles
enshrining bleed, vote and combat options for each clan are available,
and are a useful way of thinking about such. Take that to a more
detailed level and you have a close approximation of a more useful
'ranking' system.)

>>>>I don't think that there are any justifiable conditions for a 3-2 split
>>deal.>>
>>
>>And I think you are misaken. I have presented a situation where I feel that
>>such a deal is justified many times, and there are no rules that
>>contradict me.
>
>So far as VEKN tournaments are concerned, they are rules 5.1 Cheating
>and 5.2. Unsportsmanlike Conduct.

It is certainly true that there are situations where a proposed 3-2 deal
will fall under these rules.

It is also clear - from LSJ's posts - that there are, in his
authoritative view, that there are situations where this will also not
be the case, however difficult these may be to attain. A lot of the
current situation has been nullified with the introduction of the game-
win rule (now in force, folks), though certainly not all. Two decks
will both need and want to go for a game win to advance so there is a
*lot* more difference between a 3-2 split now and previously since only
one person can get a game-win (of which there are only a maximum of 3
available to a deck in most tournaments), whereas a deck being one VP
down with a possibility of up to 10 on other tables (again, assuming a 3
round+final set-up) is less significant and certainly acts to get more
VPs than it currently has.

Most such proposed deals will have a situation where one player would
have to give up their chance of a game win. In such an instance, a
judge can be asked to rule. However, it is far from impossible that all
given situations will necessitate such - even under the old V:EKN rules,
the idea that a player could not ever be in a situation where their fate
was decided was not true.

>In Shadowfist, there are tournament systems for allocating places.
>These are usually based upon that game's equivalent of victory points,
>feng shui sites. I don't like to use these because they encourage
>players to play for a place rather than to win.

This is certainly a valid objection (even if, in the grand scheme of
things, you're in a minority). It is clear that Shadowfist was designed
on all-or-nothing situation, from what I can tell and the (extremely
little) experience I have of the game.

However, Jyhad was always designed - from the beginning - with the
predator-prey/VP dynamic for all practical purposes. This acts to
encourage certain styles of play that the game was designed around. In
the same way as trying to attach ranking to Shadowfist violates a number
of the design principles - in that it certainly seems possible in many
such games that a certainly style of deck could function 'well' whilst
evading or, at least, slightly foxing the ranking criteria because the
game was not set up with that in mind - trying to remove the scoring
system from V:TES similarly violates it. The game is and always was set
up to give players scores, determining a winner in the process.

>When players stop
>trying to win then the game is spoilt and the same is true of VTES.

Potentially true, for any given group of people. It is unlikely that
any person turns up to a competitive tournament aiming to play for
second (and those who do not play competitively can potentially be dealt
with by a judge). However, what you are asking is that a person who
sees that they cannot win because of a number of facets cannot use their
skills at diplomacy to advance their position at that table - seemingly
based on a desire to create an all-or-nothing situation because of your
personal disposition towards such a set of scoring criteria. Diplomacy
was built into the game from the very start. Garfield knew that in
*any* multiplayer game it was going to be impossible to prevent. So the
cards and rules were designed to fight the diplomacy, but not render it
entirely useless.

You appear to be arguing for the removal of another fundamental design
tenet.

It seems clear that Jyhad is not, was never designed to be and would
require a fundamental reworking to be the game you envisage. There
would potentially be nothing wrong with that game. It's simply not this
game.

You don't want Shadowfist reworked into a scored, second-place-potential
game like Jyhad. Why should we want Jyhad reworked into an all-or-
nothing game like Shadowfist?

Lots of players keep the possibility to table-talk as a very important
aspect of this game, which differentiates this game from most other
CCGs. This group include me, my friends and most of other VTES players
I know.

If look at this through economics point of view there is the issue of
oligopolies and monopolies. It's important to regulate monopolies and
oligopolies when there exists a situation where:
forming an alliance results directly in a consistent winning situation
(on the expense of others) in the starting position AND there doesn't
exist ANY incentives to break that alliance later on. (There are lots
of other situations that can be considered bad - like for instance
where some players on the market clearly cannot do anything to gain
good position etc.)

These hold only in when really collusive behaviour is seen (two people
that have agreed beforehand to make decks that support each other and
that it doesn't matter to them which positions they get as long one or
the other wins).

But even as the RL markets are as they are the regulation is done by
external force (government body etc.) with the aid of regulations
(antitrust laws)- but alliances and DEALS are not banned all together,
because this would hinder the development of the markets.

So it is true that some (a very small fraction of VTES players) could
gain unjustified benefit from the current open atmosphere (collusion).
But IMHO Judges are enough of a solution to hinder collusive
behaviour. Normal table talk and short-term deals are really fine -
and so are table split deals if they are done in a situation which is
clearly impossible for the players participating.

You can always choose the events you take part in. It's quite

Andrew wrote:
>>So what is your method then? So far as I can see, your method is to
look at the deck and perform some sort of mental assessment in the
light of your experience of the game. This is not objective.>>

The whole original point of this tangent was that there is nothing preventing
folks from playing badly, and playing a bad deck at a tournament is playing
badly. Can you numerically prove that a given deck is bad? Probably not.
However, some decks are simply a bad idea, and playing them in a tournament is
tantamount to playing to lose from the get go. Such a deck does not need to
consist of 90 Tourtured Confessions to be a bad deck. You can't prevent someone
from playing a bad deck, nor can you prevent someone from making stupid
strategy decisions or using bad tactics. If you can't prevent someone from
doing this, you can't prevent someone from outsting themself for whatever
reason.

>>So far as VEKN tournaments are concerned, they are rules 5.1 Cheating
and 5.2. Unsportsmanlike Conduct.>>

But you are mistaken. There is nothing saying that making a deal to get 2 VPs
instead of 0 VPs is cheating--how is that cheating? What rule does it break?

How is it unsportsmanlike? You are making a deal to get more VPs than you would
otherwise, therfore trying to do your best possible in a given game. As trying
to win (the stated goal of the game) is tantamount to trying to do the best
possible in a given game, you are doing what you are supposed to do.

There are some situations where you are virtually assured 0 VPs unless you do
something like a table split deal. If making this deal gets you 2 VPs instead
of 0 VPs, you are playing to do the best possible in the situation.

>>In Shadowfist, there are tournament systems for allocating places.>>

Yeah, but they are highly questionable and somewhat nebulous. And basically a
bad idea.

>>These are usually based upon that game's equivalent of victory points,
feng shui sites. I don't like to use these because they encourage
players to play for a place rather than to win.>>

They don't really, 'cause getting that second place is so highly mutable and
random--you gain and lose "VPs" all the time. You could be in "second place" at
the end of your turn, and be in last place (due to being bombed back to the
stone age) before your next turn even starts. Thus, trying for that second
place is really difficult, and helping someone get first place in no way
assures you second. In Fist, essentially, someone wins and the other three
people are given a nominal ranking based on very fluid factors. You can't
realistically at some point claim "I can't win, but I can get second if I help
*you* win"--there are rarely, if ever situations where a given player will be
unable to win, but capable of coming in secnd place.

Thus, limited, if any, incentive to play for second place. You can pretty much
always pull a win out in Fist, as it is far more dynamic in terms of player
interaction--the multi player aspect is far more of a factor than in VTES. In
VTES, not so much.

>>When players stop trying to win then the game is spoilt and the same is true
of VTES.>>

I agree, yet splitting a table 3/2 when you are assured 0 VPs otherwise is not
playing not to win. It is necessary for a game of VTES to work to play to win.
However, if you are in a losing position and assured 0 VPs otherwise, making a
deal to get 2 VPs is optimizing your position and playing to do better than you
would have otherwise.
